summary: Mexico lets citizens of more than 60 countries and territories — including the US, Canada, the UK, the EU, Japan and much of Latin America — visit visa-free for up to 180 days, waives its visa for anyone holding a valid US visa, and offers a free electronic authorization (SAE) for air arrivals from Russia, Turkey and Ukraine.

primarySources.name: Instituto Nacional de Migración (INM) — National Migration Institute
Secretaría de Relaciones Exteriores (SRE) — Mexican consular network

passportValidity.text: Mexico requires your passport to be valid for the entire duration of your stay; there is no formal 6-month rule, but airlines sometimes apply one — extra validity is safer.

source.name: Instituto Nacional de Migración (INM)

travelInsurance.text: Travel insurance is not an entry requirement, but private healthcare — the standard for visitors — must be paid for, so medical coverage is strongly recommended.

source.name: Instituto Nacional de Migración (INM)

onwardTicket.text: Not a formal entry requirement, but immigration officers and airlines may ask for proof of return or onward travel and where you will stay.

source.name: Instituto Nacional de Migración (INM)

proofOfFunds.text: No fixed amount is set, but officers may ask about your funds, accommodation and purpose of visit when deciding how many days to grant.

source.name: Instituto Nacional de Migración (INM)

declarations.name: FMM (Forma Migratoria Múltiple) — being phased out
declarations.text: The paper FMM tourist card has been phased out at all major airports and most land crossings in favor of a passport stamp or digital record. If you receive a stamp, note the number of days written in it — that, not 180, is your permitted stay. Some minor land crossings may still issue an FMM.

source.name: Instituto Nacional de Migración (INM)

currencyLimits.text: Cash and monetary instruments over 10,000 USD (or equivalent) must be declared on arrival and departure; failing to declare can mean seizure and fines.

source.name: ANAM — Declaración de dinero (cash declaration)

notes: Adults (18 and over) may bring in duty-free up to 20 packs of cigarettes, 25 cigars or 200 g of tobacco, plus up to 3 liters of alcoholic beverages and 6 liters of wine.
Firearms and ammunition are strictly prohibited without a Mexican permit — even a single forgotten cartridge can lead to arrest.

payments.text: Cards are accepted in hotels, malls and formal restaurants in cities and resorts; markets, street food, small shops, buses and many taxis are cash-only. Carry small peso notes — large bills can be hard to change.

safety.text: Safety varies dramatically by state: major tourist areas are heavily policed and generally trouble-free, while several states carry do-not-travel advisories due to organized crime. Check the state-by-state US advisory for your exact route and avoid intercity road travel at night.

source.name: UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office — Mexico travel advice

bestTimeToVisit.text: November to April is the dry season across most of the country — sunny and mild, avoiding both the summer rains and the June–November hurricane season on the coasts.

tips.text: Mexico is not one uniform risk level. A handful of states are under do-not-travel advisories while the main tourist corridors are fine. Check advice for each state on your itinerary, not just the country page.
Entry to Mexico is free for visa-free tourists. The paper FMM has been phased out at airports, and third-party websites selling "Mexico tourist cards" or "entry registrations" are unnecessary.
180 days is the legal maximum, not a guarantee. Check the number of days the officer writes in your stamp before leaving the desk, and ask for more if your trip needs it.
Do not drink tap water anywhere in Mexico. Use bottled or purified water (garrafón), including for brushing teeth in less touristy areas.

faq.question: Do US citizens need a visa for Mexico?
faq.answer: No. US citizens can visit Mexico visa-free for tourism or business for up to 180 days. The immigration officer decides the exact number of days and records it in your passport stamp. It is no longer an automatic 180.

faq.question: I have a US visa — do I still need a Mexican visa?
faq.answer: No. Any traveler holding a valid visa for the United States (or Canada, the UK, Japan or a Schengen country) is exempt from the Mexican visitor visa and can enter visa-free for up to 180 days, regardless of nationality.

faq.question: Is the FMM tourist card still required?
faq.answer: The paper FMM has been phased out at all major airports and most land crossings — your passport stamp (or digital record) is now the proof of legal entry. Note the number of days written in the stamp; that is your permitted stay. A few minor land crossings may still issue the paper form.

faq.question: What is Mexico's SAE electronic authorization?
faq.answer: The SAE (Sistema de Autorización Electrónica) is a free online authorization that lets citizens of Russia, Turkey and Ukraine fly to Mexico without a consular visa. It is valid for 30 days for a single air entry, allows a stay of up to 180 days, and cannot be used at land or sea borders.

faq.question: How long can I stay in Mexico as a tourist?
faq.answer: Up to 180 days if the immigration officer grants it — officers now often stamp shorter periods matched to your ticket and plans. The days granted appear in your entry stamp; overstaying leads to fines on exit.
